background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: So when you think about the period since Dodd-Frank, how do you think those regulations have distorted American economic life? ground_truth: Yes, you know, Fannie and Freddie should be privatized and mortgage should be just like any other loan in the system. But I think if you look at the rise of SPACs there, you know, Dodd-Frank made it really difficult to become a public company. You had to fill out all you had. You had tremendous regulations on you. And many companies just said, look, let me stay under the radar screen. I'll stay private. Private equity will fund me. I need some more money. Hopefully they can they can help me out. And it was a very dramatic decline in the number of IPOs. SPACs are really a way around some of the Dodd-Frank rules where you don't have to you know, you're allowed to say you don't have to disclose what your future revenues are going to be. And you don't have to and you're allowed to say we may lose all our money. You don't have to say we may have to lose all our money like you do in an IPO. So all these entrepreneurs said, oh, I can finally come out without a lot of the rules and regulations. And we've seen a burst of activity. New companies, new ideas coming forward. And we don't really need SPACs. We just need a change to the IPO rules that you just say you're an adult. This is a risky business. Give me, you know, give me some money. You may lose it all. That's life. Or you may get rich and you're an adult and that's it. That is what needs to be fixed so that we can get more and more enterprises going. And if we can make it as easy as possible for entrepreneurs to raise money, we will have all these. Great projects. We will have the Zooms of the world and we'll have, you know, Teslas because it's easier to raise money in the United States than anywhere else. Why we would want to do anything to discourage that is beyond me. But that's exactly what Dodd-Frank does.
